la:verb:excido.gloss: to fall out, from or down, tumble to the ground, collapse, break down, drop
senses: to fall out, from or down, tumble to the ground, collapse, break down, drop
to fall out or from involuntarily, slip out, escape
to differ from someone's opinion, disagree with, dissent
to be lost or forgotten, pass away, perish, disappear
to lose oneself, fail; faint, swoon
to slip out, away or escape from memory, i.e. forget
to be deprived of, miss, fail to obtain, forfeit, lose
la:verb:excido.html:
ex-cĭdo, cĭdi, 3, v. n.
cado
,
to fall out or down, to fall from (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense).
Lit.
In gen.: quod (animal) cum ex utero elapsum excidit, : sol excidisse mihi e mundo videtur,: gladii de manibus exciderunt,; cf. ; ; for which also: inter manus (urna), and: a digitis (ansa),: Palinurus exciderat puppi,; cf. arce,: equis,: num qui nummi exciderunt, here, tibi, quod sic terram Obtuere?; cf. ; ; : volvae excidunt,.—Poet.: ita vinclis Excidet aut in aquas tenues dilapsus abibit,will slip out of the fetters,: in flumen (elephanti, sc. e rate),: cum Herculis pertractanti arma sagitta excidisset in pedem,: ante pedes (lingua resecta),.—
In partic., of a lot, to fall of come out (very rare): ut cujusque sors exciderat,; and hence, transf.: nominibus in urnam conjectis, citari quod primum sorte nomen excidit,.
Trop.
In gen., to fall out involuntarily, fall from, slip out, escape: verbum ex ore alicujus,; cf.: vox excidit ore: Venisti tandem, etc.,: tantumque nefas patrio excidit ore?; cf.: scelus ore tuo,: quod verbum tibi non excidit, ut saepe fit, fortuito,; cf. ; ; : libellus me imprudente et invito excidit,escaped me without my knowledge or desire,; cf. : vox horrenda per auras excidit,: et pariter vultusque deo plectrumque colorque Excidit,; cf. : ut quodammodo victoria e manibus excideret,: (versus) qui in breves excidunt,i. e. which close, terminate,.—Poet.: in vitium libertas excidit, qs. falls away, sinks, = delabitur, .—
In partic. *
To dissent, differ from any one's opinion: ego ab Archilocho excido, Lucil. ap. .—
To pass away, be lost, perish, disappear: neque enim verendum est, ne quid excidat aut ne quid in terram defluat,: primo miser excidit aevo, (4, 6, 7 M.): nec vera virtus, cum semel excidit, etc.,: at non ingenio quaesitum nomen ab aevo Excidet, (4, 1, 64 M.): excidit omnis luctus,: ne Tarentinae quidem arcis excidit memoria,; cf. the foll.—Esp.
To fail, faint, swoon, lose one's self: excidit illa metu, rupitque novissima verba,; cf.: ut scias quemadmodum nunquam excidam mihi, lose control of myself (through drink), Sen. de Ira, 3, 14, 1: quis me dolori reddit? quam bene excideram mihi!—
To slip out, escape from the memory: excidere de memoria,: exciderat pacis mentio ex omnium animis,; cf. animo,; ; and pectore,: o miram memoriam, Pomponi, tuam! at mihi ista exciderant,; so with dat.: quae cogitatio, cum mihi non omnino excidisset, etc.,; ; ; ; ; 4 (5), 7, 15 et saep.; cf. with a subjectclause: non excidit mihi, scripsisse me, etc.,.—Absol.: quid? non haec varietas mira est, excidere proxima, vetera inhaerere? hesternorum immemores acta pueritiae recordari,; ; ; 4, 5, 2; cf. with inf. clause: si calore dicendi vitare id excidisset,; and with ut: excidit, ut peterem, etc.,i. e. I forgot to beg,.—Rarely transf. to the person: excidens,who forgets, forgetful,: palam moneri excidentis est,.—
(Ex) aliquā re, of persons, to be deprived of, to lose, miss, forfeit (esp. freq. since the Aug. per.; in Cic. not at all): ex familia,: uxore,to be disappointed of,: regno,: quem si non tenuit, magnis tamen excidit ausis,failed in a great attempt,; cf.: fine medicinae,: genere,: qui apud privatos judices plus petendo formula excidissent, i. e. who lost their suits (for the usual cadere formulā or

causā; v. cado, II.),; .

la:verb:excido#2.gloss: to cut or hew out, off, or down
senses: to cut or hew out, off, or down
to raze, demolish, lay waste, destroy
to cut out, hollow out, excavate

la:verb:excuso.gloss: to excuse, allege in excuse, free from a charge
senses: to excuse, allege in excuse, free from a charge
to cite as an excuse or pretext or justification
la:verb:excuso.html:
ex-cūso (excuss-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
causa; cf. accuso, from ad-causa; qs. to release from a charge, to free from blame; hence
,
to excuse a person or thing.
Lit.
With a personal object, aliquem alicui: Atticae meae velim me ita excuses, ut omnem culpam in te transferas,; cf.: aliquem alicui per litteras,; and: his omnibus me vehementer excusatum volo,.—With quod: Titium excusavit Vespa Terentius, quod eum brachium fregisse diceret,: Libo excusat Bibulum, quod is, etc.,: primum me tibi excuso in eo ipso, in quo te accuso,: se de aliqua re,: de me excusando apud Apuleium, dederam ad te litteras,: se alicui,; et saep.—In pass.: cura, ut excuser morbi causa in dies singulos,: si citatus judex non responderit excuseturque Areopagites esse, etc., excuses himself as being, etc., : dixi, cur excusatus abirem,: apud Appuleium in dies ut excuser videbis,: me excusatum esse apud Appuleium a Laterense,.—
With inanim. or abstr. objects, to excuse, apologize for: Varroni memineris excusare tarditatem litterarum mearum,: habitum permutatum,: palliolum, fascias, etc. (sola valetudo),: commentarios,: missos ignes,; dolorem,: toros,: reditum Agrippinae ob imminentem partum et hiemem,her not returning,.
Transf.
Aliquid (alicui), i. q. se propter aliquid, to allege in excuse, to plead as an excuse, to excuse one's self with.
With acc.: propinquitatem excusavit,: morbum,: inopiam (with calamitatem queri),: valetudinem,: imbecillitatem,: vires,: diversa, et saep.: ille Philippo Excusare laborem et mercenaria vincla, Quod non mane domum venisset, etc.,: dictatorem se apud patres excusare solitum,: aliquid apud aliquem,; .—Pass.: quae apud Vitellium excusanda erant,: excusata necessitas praesentium,: excusata rei familiaris mediocritate,: excusatus languor faucium, propter quem non adesset, et saep.—
With an object-clause: si prehensi sumus, excusemus, ebrios Nos fecisse, etc., (but in , the correct reading is incusato, v. Ritschl ad h. l.): excusanti, minus datum ad occultandam facinoris invidiam, ; .—
Aliquem ab aliqua re, aliqua re, or alicui rei, to excuse, absolve one from any thing; to discharge, dispense with one (postAug.): a coepta (tutela) excusari,: collegarum filiorum tutela excusari,; cf. : cui excusari mallet,. 12; . But (class.): se de aliqua re: legati venerunt, qui se de superioris temporis consilio excusarent, quod, etc.,.—
Se ab aliqua re, to shelter, protect one's self from any thing (post-class.): ut invicom se a calore excusent (plantae),. —Hence,
Aliquid aliqua re, to compensate, atone for any thing (post-Aug. and rare): nefas armis,; ; .—Hence, excūsātus, a, um, P. a., excused (postAug. and rare): hoc et ego excusatior, si forte sum lapsus, et tu dignior laude,; : excusatissimus essem, etiamsi, etc.,.—Adv.: excūsātē, without blame, excusably: fieri id videtur excusate,.—Comp.: quod exoratus excusatius facies,; ; .

la:noun:excusatio.html:
excūsātĭo (excuss-), ōnis, f.
excuso
,
an excusing, excuse (freq. and class.); constr. with obj. or subj. gen., absol., with cur, quominus, etc.
With gen. obj.: peccati,: intermissionis litterarum,: valent apud me excusationes injuriae tuae,.—
With gen. subj.: pauci ejusdem generis addit cum excusatione Pompeii conjuncta (shortly before: velle Pompeium se Caesari purgatum),.—With both constructions: excusatio Ser. Sulpicii legationis obeundae,.—
With a causal gen. (freq.): hic dies summa'st apud me inopiae excusatio,: excusatio vel pietatis, vel necessitatis, vel aetatis,; cf. adolescentiae,: me neque honoris neque aetatis excusatio vindicat a labore,: aetatis,: valetudinis,: oculorum,:

familiaris funeris, : amicitiae,: necessitatis,: summae stultitiae, et saep.—

Absol.: turpis enim excusatio est si quis contra rem publicam se amici causa fecisse fateatur,: illa perfugia, quae sumunt sibi ad excusationem,: (Sappho) dat tibi justam excusationem,: libenter Caesar petentibus Aeduis dat veniam excusationemque accipit,: triduum disputationibus excusationibusque extrahitur, et saep.—(ε) With cur and quominus: accipio excusationem tuam, qua usus es, cur, etc.,: nemini civi ullam, quominus adesset, satis justam excusationem esse visam,.—(ζ) With acc. and inf.: habent excusationem legitimam, exsilii causa solum vertisse nec esse postea restitutos,.—(η) With kindr. accus.: ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis,.—
Transf., a being excused, a release, discharge from any thing (post-class.): tria onera tutelarum dant excusationem, (De excusationibus), 3; cf.: omnibus excusatio a tutela competit, et saep. (vid. the whole title).

la:verb:excludo.gloss: to shut out; cut off, remove, separate from something
senses: to shut out; cut off, remove, separate from something
to drive out, press, thrust or take out
la:verb:excludo.html:
ex-clūdo, si, sum, 3 (
perf. sync. exclusti for exclusisti, ) [cludo, claudo], to shut out, exclude; to cut off, remove, separate from any thing (class.).
Lit.
In gen.: aliquem a portu et perfugio, : aliquem ab re frumentaria,: aliquem ab acie,: Gaditani Poenos moenibus excluserunt,: nulla exclusura dolentes Janua,.—With inanimate objects: spissa ramis laurea fervidos Excludet ictus (solis),: aquam quae exundante palude in agrum refluere solet,: exclusere diem telis,shut out, obscured,: Euphrates Armeniae regiones a Cappadocia excludens,separating,.—
Esp., to shut out, refuse to receive a visitor: quo pacto excludi, quaeso, potis est planius, quam exclusus nunc sum,: ego excludor, ille recipitur,; : aliquem foras,; : quae me non excludet ab se, sed apud se occludet domi,; cf.: ut ab illa excludar, huc concludar,; ; ; cf.: priusquam Caesar me abs te excludere posset, Pomp. ap. B. 1.—
Transf.
To drive out, to put, press, thrust, or take out: excludito mihi hercle oculum, si dedero,i. e. to knock out,: vel oculum exclude,: gemmam,: liquorem,: pallio caput,.—
In partic. of birds, to hatch their young: volucres Ova relinquebant, exclusae tempore verno,; cf.: gallinae avesque reliquae, cum ex ovis pullos excluserint, etc.,: pullos,; ; ; —And transf., by way of pun, to the pupils of the rhetorician Corax (raven): Coracem istum patiamur pullos suos excludere in nido, qui evolent, clamatores odiosi ac molesti,.—
To make prominent (eccl. Lat.), = eminere, ; ; cf. Aug. Spir. et Litt. § 17.—*
To close, complete: volumen,fin.
Trop., to exclude, except, remove, hinder, prevent: Crassus tres legatos decernit, nec excludit Pompeium,: excludi ab omni doctrina,; cf.: exclusit illum a re publica,: ab hereditate fraterna excludi,; cf. also: ne anni tempore a navigatione excluderetur,: ut reditu in Asiam excluderetur,: exceptione excludi,: multas actiones praetoriis exceptionibus,: angustiis temporis excluduntur omnes,: tempore exclusus,hindered, prevented,: diei tempore exclusus,: si qui se in hoc judicium forte projecerint, excluditote eorum cupiditatem,: servitutem, Lucil. ap. : consuetudinem libere dicendi,.—Hence, * exclūsus, a, um, P. a., shut out, locked out: nunc ego sum exclusissimus,.

la:verb:excogito.gloss: to contrive, devise or invent (by thinking)
senses: to contrive, devise or invent (by thinking)
to think up or create out of nothing
la:verb:excogito.html:
ex-cōgĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to find out by thinking, to contrive, devise, invent (freq. and class.; cf.: comminiscor, simulo, confingo, fingo, etc.): quid enim mali aut sceleris fingi aut excogitari potest, quod non ille conceperit?: ad haec igitur cogita, mi Attice, vel potius excogita,: quid igitur causae excogitari potest, cur? etc.,: novam interregni ineundi rationem,: aliquid dignum dono deorum aut efficere aut excogitare,: multa praeterea generatim ad avaritiam excogitabantur,: aliquid ad ornatum portarum, etc.,: o callidos homines! o rem excogitatam!: quicquid omnino excogitari contra potest,: res ab illis dicta, non a nobis excogitata,: in rebus excogitandis (opp. gerendis),fin.—Impers. with ut: excogitatum est a quibusdam ut, etc.,; cf. with a subject-sentence: cum recenti fico salis vice caseo vesci nuper excogitatum est,.—
Transf., to name: Alpes Poeninas,.—Hence, * excōgĭtātus, a, um, P. a., sought out, choice: excogitatissimae hostiae,.

la:verb:excipio.gloss: to take out, extract, pull out
senses: to take out, extract, pull out
to follow after, succeed a thing in time or the order of succession
to answer, reply, take up the discussion in succession
to understand (in the sense of taking in or receiving knowledge/meaning)
la:verb:excipio.html:
ex-cĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3, v. a.
capio
.
(With the notion of the ex predominating.) To take or draw out.
Lit. (rarely): aliquem e mari, to draw out, fish out, ap. (Rep. 4, 8, 8 Baiter): vidulum (e mari),: dens manu, forcipe,: telum (e vulnere),: clipeum cristasque rubentes Excipiam sorti,to withdraw, exempt,.—
Trop.
In gen.: servitute exceptus, withdrawn, i. e. rescued from slavery, : nihil jam cupiditati, nihil libidini exceptum,exempt,.—
In partic.
To except, make an exception of (freq. and class.): hosce ego homines excipio et secerno libenter,: qui (Democritus) ita sit ausus ordiri: Haec loquor de universis. Nihil excipit, de quo non profiteatur,; cf. : Lacedaemonii ipsi, cum omnia concedunt in amore juvenum praeter stuprum, tenui sane muro dissaepiunt id, quod excipiunt,: senex talos elidi jussit conservis meis: sed me excepit,.—With ne: Licinia lex, quae non modo eum, qui, etc.... sed etiam collegas ejus, cognatos, affines excipit, ne eis ea potestas curatiove mandetur,; so in legal limitations,; ; see also exceptio.—With ut, : excepi de antiquis praeter Xenophanem neminem,: ut in summis tuis laudibus excipiant unam iracundiam,: dolia, in horreis defossa, si non sint nominatim in venditione excepta, etc.,; so .—In the abl. absol.: omnium mihi videor, exceptis, Crasse, vobis duobus, eloquentissimos audisse Ti. et C. Sempronios,you two excepted,; cf.: vos hortor, ut ita virtutem locetis, ut eā exceptā nihil amicitia praestabilius esse putetis,: exceptā sapientiā,. —Neutr. absol.: excepto, quod non simul esses, cetera laetus,: excepto, si obscena nudis nominibus enuntientur,; ; ; .—Hence,
Jurid. t. t., said of the defendant, to except, to make a legal exception to the plaintiff's statement: verum est, quod qui excipit, probare debeat, quod excipitur,; so : adversus aliquem, et saep.; cf. exceptio and the authorities there cited.—
In an oration, a law, etc., to express by name, to make particular mention of, to state expressly (rare, and perh. not anteAug.): cum Graecos Italia pellerent, excepisse medicos,: vites in tantum sublimes, ut vindemitor auctoratus rogum ac tumulum excipiat, expressly stipulates for (in case he should fall and break his neck), .
(With the notion of the verb predominating.) To take a thing to one's self (in a good or bad sense), to catch, capture, take, receive.
Lit.
In gen.: sanguinem paterā,; cf. : e longinquo sucum,: labentem excepit,: se in pedes, to take to one's feet, i. e. spring to the ground, : filiorum extremum spiritum ore,; cf.: tunicis fluentibus auras,: omnium tela,; so, tela,: vulnera,; cf.: vulnus ore,; and: plagae genus in se,: o terram illam beatam, quae hunc virum exceperit!; cf.: hunc (Mithridatem) in timore et fuga Tigranes excepit, : aliquem benigno vultu,; cf. also: hic te polenta excipiet,: aliquem epulis,: multos ex fuga dispersos excipiunt,. alios vagos per hiberna milites excipiebant, : speculator, exceptus a juvenibus mulcatur, : cf. Planc. ap. : servos in pabulatione,: incautum,: (uri) mansuefieri ne parvuli quidem excepti possunt,: aprum latitantem,: caprum insidiis,: fugientes feras,: aprum, feram venabulo,; et saep.—
Of inanimate subjects: postero die patenti itinere Priaticus campus eos excepit,received them,: silva tum excepit ferum,; . —
In partic.
To come next to, to follow after, succeed a thing: linguam ad radices ejus haerens excipit stomachus,: quinque milia passuum proxima intercedere itineris campestris; inde excipere loca aspera et montuosa,: alios alii deinceps,—Poet.: porticus excipiebat Arcton,i. e. was turned to the north, looked towards the north,.—
In medic. lang.: aliquid aliqua re, to take something in something, i. e. mixed with something: quae (medicamenta) excipiuntur cerato ex rosa facto,; ; ; 12 et saep.—
Trop.
In gen., to take or catch up, to intercept: genus divinationis naturale, quod animus arripit aut excipit extrinsecus ex divinitate,; cf.: posteaquam vidit, illum excepisse laudem ex eo, quod,i. e. obtained,: subire coëgit et excipere pericula, to take upon one's self, to receive, support, sustain (the figure being taken from the reception of an enemy's blows or shots), ; cf.: Germani celeriter phalange facta impetus gladiorum exceperunt,; so, impetus,: vim frigorum hiememque,: labores magnos, et saep.: excipimus nova illa cum favore et sollicitudine,receive,: verba risu,: praecepta ad excipiendas hominum voluntates,for taking captive,: invidiam,to draw upon one's self,.—
Of inanim. or abstr. subjects: quae (sublicae) cum omni opere conjunctae vim fluminis exciperent,; : quid reliquis accideret, qui quosque eventus exciperent,i. e. would befall, overtake them,; ; .—
In partic.
To catch with the ear, esp. eagerly or secretly, to catch up, listen to, overhear: maledicto nihil facilius emittitur, nihil citius excipitur,; : assensu populi excepta vox consulis,: ad has excipiendas voces speculator missus,; ; : laudem avidissimis auribus excipit,: notis quoque excipere velocissime solitum,i. e. to write down in shorthand,: rumores,; cf. voces,: sermonem eorum,: furtivas notas,.—
To follow after, to succeed a thing in time or the order of succession (cf. above, A. 2. a.): tristem hiemem pestilens aestas excepit,: Herculis vitam et virtutem immortalitas excepisse dicitur,: violis succedit rosa: rosam cyanus excipit, cyanum amarantus,: excipit Pompilium Numam Tullus Hostilius,: hunc (locutum) Labienus excepit,.—Absol.: turbulentior inde annus excepit,succeeded, followed,; : re cognita tantus luctus excepit, ut, etc.,.—Hence,
Transf.: aliquid, to continue, prolong a thing: memoriam illius viri excipient omnes anni consequentes,; : vices alicujus,.— Poet. with inf., .

la:verb:excurro.html:
ex-curro, cŭcurri (; et saep.;
less freq. curri,), cursum, 3, v. n. and a.
Neut., to run out or forth, to hasten forwards.
Lit.: cum se excucurrisse illuc frustra sciverit,: excurrat aliquis, qui hoc tantum mali filio suo nuntiet,: mandavi utrique eorum, ut ante ad me excurrerent, ut tibi obviam prodire possem,: excurristi a Neapoli, Caes. ap. P.: dum panes et cetera in navem parantur, excurro in Pompeianum,make an excursion,; so of a long journey: in Graeciam,; of eagerness in applauding a speaker: proni atque succincti ad omnem clausulam non exsurgunt modo, verum etiam excurrunt,: in crucem,to go to destruction, go to the devil,: ad hominem Dei,.—
In partic., milit. t. t., to sally forth, to make an excursion or irruption: sine signis omnibus portis,: in fines Romanos excucurrerunt populandi magis quam justi more belli, Drak. N. cr.: Carthago excurrere ex Africa videbatur,: excursurus cum valida manu fuerat,.—
Transf., of inanim. or abstr. things.
In gen., to go forth, issue forth: fons ex summo montis cacumine excurrens,; : nec recisis qui a lateribus excurrant pampinis,shoot forth,: quorum animi spretis corporibus evolant atque excurrunt foras,.—
In partic.
Of localities, to run out, project, extend: ab intimo sinu paeninsula excurrit,: Sicania tribus excurrit in aequora linguis,: promontorium in altum, Drak.: dorsum montis in Persidem,: promontorium per Creticum mare,.—
In specifications of measure, to be over and above, to exceed (late Lat.; cf. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 435): decem (auri pondo) et quod excurrit,and something over,: viginti et quod excurrit annorum pax,of twenty years and upwards,. —
Trop., to run or spread out, to extend, display itself: campus, in quo excurrere virtus posset,: quid est, cur insistere orationem malint quam cum sententia pariter excurrere? qs. to keep pace with, : ne oratio excurrat longius,to run out to too great length, be prolix,: extra ordinem excurrens tractatio,: paeone dochmioque, quorum prior in quatuor, secundus in quinque (syllabas) excurrit,: praecoces germinationes,: in hos quoque studiorum secessus excurrit, qs. makes excursions, : in pericula,: quia in hoc tempus excurrit donationis eventus, quo,extends,: quaedam (in periodo) quasi decurtata ... productiora alia et quasi immoderatius excurrentia, running out, stretched out (the figure being taken from places which run out or project, v. above), .—
To run out, end, terminate, of verses: in quatuor syllabas,.—
Act. (very rare).
To run through a place; trop.: prope jam excurso spatio,; cf. Lachm. ad .—
To pass over, omit something in speaking: a quo multa improbe sed venuste dicta, ne modum excedam, excurro,, p. 374 Bip.

la:verb:exclamo.gloss: to exclaim or shout, cry or call out
senses: to exclaim or shout, cry or call out
la:verb:exclamo.html:
ex-clāmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.
Neut., to call or cry aloud, to call or cry out, to exclaim: cum exclamasset Laelius,: in stadio cursores exclamant quam maxime possunt,; cf. : majus,: contiones saepe exclamare vidi, cum apte verba cecidissent,i. e. to applaud loudly,; cf. .—Pass. impers.: quoties exclamandum erit, lateris conatus sit ille, non capitis,; .—
Transf.
Of inanim. and abstr. things (postAug.): apud hunc (oratorem) patria ipsa exclamabit,: ignis exclamat,i. e. crackles aloud, makes a noise,: dominae femur exclamare coëgit,: quae (verba) aut maxime exclamant, aut sono sunt jucundissima,: minus exclamantes syllabae,.—
Of a sound made with musical instruments: sacris tubis,; cf. 3, 54; 4, 40.—
Act., to call out, say aloud, exclaim.
With inanim. objects.
With an object-clause, in oratio recta: ibi nescio quis maxima Voce exclamat: Alcumena, adest auxilium, ne time,: cf.: non possum quin exclamem: Euge, euge, etc., (quoted ): mihi libet exclamare, Pro deum, etc.,; ; ; ; ; —With acc. and inf.: hic exclamat, eum sibi esse sodalem,; .—
With ut: quas (geometricas formas) ut vidisset, exclamavisse, ut bono essent animo, videre enim se hominum vestigia, etc.,: ut equites desilirent,.—
With acc.: quaedam,to utter,: multa memoria digna,.—
With personal objects, to call upon: voce clara exclamat uxorem tuam,: M. Brutus cruentum pugionem tenens Ciceronem exclamavit, Anton. ap. : aliquem suo nomine,.
la:verb:exclamo.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and a.

la:verb:excudo.html:
ex-cūdo, di, sum, 3, v. a.,
to strike, beat or hammer out.
Lit.: silici scintillam,: ignem,.—
Transf., to hatch out: pullos ex ovis,; cf. ; ; : anseres aliena ova non excudunt,i. e. do not hatch them,; § 4; 3, 9, 2; .—
To forge, mould: excudent alii spirantia mollius aera,.—
In gen., to prepare, make any thing: ceras,.—
Trop., of a writing, to compose: excudam aliquid Ἡρακλείδειον, ; ; .

la:verb:excito.gloss: to call forth: to rouse, awaken, summon
senses: to call forth: to rouse, awaken, summon
to bring forth: to raise, build
to bring out: to encourage, revive, excite, stimulate, set in motion
la:verb:excito.html:
excĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. freq. a.
excio
,
to call out or forth, to bring or send out, to wake or rouse up (freq. and class.; cf.: provoco, evoco; irrito, lacesso, invito).
Lit.: unde (Acherunte) animae excitantur obscura umbra, Poëta ap. : aliquem a portu,: aliquem huc foras,: si excitatus fuerit de spectaculis,turned out, expelled,: dormientes spectatores e somno,to wake up,; cf.: quaeso, ne me e somno excitetis,: velut dormitantes eos excitari,: patre excitato (opp. dormiente),: scuto offenso excitatus vigil,: aliquem ab inferis,to summon up,; ; : aliquem a mortuis,: non dubitavit excitare reum consularem,to call upon to stand up, to call up,: reos,; ; cf. : testes,: judicem, Cels. ap. et saep.: feras, to rouse or scare up, : cervum nemorosis latibulis,.—Prov.: aliis leporem,.—
Transf., of inanim. and abstr. things, to raise, erect: vapores, qui a sole ex aquis excitantur,: caput altius,—
In partic., with the accessory notion of making, forming, to raise, erect, build, construct: exstrui vetat (Plato) sepulcrum altius, quam, etc. ... nec e lapide excitari amplius,: turres,; : tumulum alicui,: aedificium,: urbem,: nova sarmenta cultura excitantur,are produced,: pascua in novalibus,: ignem,to kindle up, excite,; : incendium,: invalidas flammas admoto fomite,.—Poet. transf.: aras,: foculum bucca,: siser stomachum,: uvae os, stomachum,.
Trop.
In gen., to raise up, comfort; to arouse, awaken, excite, incite, stimulate, enliven: qui ab excitata fortuna ad inclinatam et prope jacentem desciscerem,erected, established,; cf.: amici jacentem animum excitare,; and with this cf. ; and: animos excitare atque inflammare ad persequendi studium,: animos omnium ad laetitiam,: aliquem ad laborem et ad laudem,; cf. : languentem labentemque populum ad decus,: aliquem ad bellum,: aliquem ad virtutem,: aliquem ad audiendum,: gallos alacritate ad canendum, et saep.: alicujus memoriam alicui excitans,reviving, renewing,: hominum studia ad utilitates nostras allicere atque excitare,: hominum studia,: salsum excitat et a taedio defendit orationem,enlivens,: fictiones personarum mire orationem excitant,; cf. : hi soni cum augenda intentione excitandi (opp. temperandi),to sharpen, pronounce strongly,: syllabam acutam,. —
In partic.
To appeal to, call upon, cite: ut nos ex annalium monimentis testis excitamus eos, etc.,: multos testis liberalitatis tuae,.—
With the accessory idea of producing (acc. to I. B. 2.), to found, cause, occasion, excite, kindle: priusquam docuero, quibus initiis ac fundamentis hae tantae summis in rebus laudes excitatae sint,; cf. : in animis hominum motum dicendo vel excitare vel sedare,: risus,: plausum,: fletum etiam inimicis,: amores,: iras,: suspicionem alicui,: varios sermones, Cael. ap. : quantas tragoedias,: vim ac dolorem bonorum omnium, et saep. —Hence, excĭtātus, a, um, P. a. (lit. excited, kindled; hence), animated, lively, vigorous, vehement, strong, loud (rare but class.): acutus et excitatus sonus,.—Comp.: clamor,: haec lumina,: schema,.—Sup.: odor,. —Adv.: excĭtāte, vigorously, briskly, brightly, vehemently.—In the comp.: fulgent gemmae,: clamitantes,.

la:verb:excello.html:
ex-cello, cellŭi, celsum, 3 (also acc. to the 2d conj.,
praes. indic. excellet, Aem. Mac. ap. P., and subj. excelleat, ap. and 896 P.), v. a. and n.
cello
.
Act., to raise up, elevate; only: recellere reclinare, et excellere in altum extollere,; and Müll.; cf. the P. a. excelsus, below.—
Neut., to rise, elevate itself (cf.: antecello, praesto, antecedo, emineo, floreo, vigeo).
Lit., only in the P. a. excellens, q. v. A.—
Trop.
In gen., to exult, be elated: animus excellit rebus secundis, Cato ap. ; .—Far more freq. (but not in Plaut. and Ter.; and in the verb. finit. not in Aug. poets),
In partic., to be eminent, to distinguish one's self for any quality above others; to surpass, excel, in a good or (less freq.) in a bad sense: ut is, qui dignitate principibus excellit facilitate infimis par esse videatur,: ut inter quos posset excellere, cum iis, etc.,: inter omnes,: super ceteros,: ante ceteros,.—With dat.: qui longe ceteris excellere pictoribus existimabatur,: quae una ceteris excellebat,; ; ; : ceteris,.—With abl.: bonā famā,: ingenio scientiāque,: animi magnitudine,: actione,: hoc genere virtutis,: dignitate,: altitudine,: candore, et saep.—With in and abl.: in arte,: in aliqua arte et facultate,: in alia parte orationis,: maxime in amicitiis expetendis colendisque,; et saep.— Absol.: excellit atque eminet vis, potestas nomenque regium,; ; ; ; ; ; (with eminere) et saep. —In a bad sense: vitiis,: cum haec (flagitia), quae excellunt, me nosse videas,—Hence,
excellens, entis, P. a., rising, overtopping.
Lit., high, lofty (very rare; not in Cic.): oppida excellentibus locis constituta, Auct. B. Hisp. 8, 4: corpore excellens,.—Far more freq. and class.,
Trop., distinguishing himself, distinguished, superior, surpassing, excellent: deos rerum omnium praestantia excellentes,: Brutus noster excellens omni genere laudis,; for which also: in omni genere,; : cujus excellens in re militari gloria,: Galba fuit inter tot aequales unus excellens,: natura excellens atque praestans,: scientia excellens atque singularis,: vir excellenti providentia,; for which: excellente ingenii magnitudine, (al. excellenti and excellentis, v. Orell. ad h. l.): studium,: pulchritudo muliebris formae,: cygnus, * et saep.—Subst.: excellentia, ōrum, n., exceptional instances: nec excellentia, sed quotidiana tractabo, § 62.—Comp.: ova excellentiora,: nihil illo (sc. Alcibiade) fuisse excellentius, vel in vitiis, vel in virtutibus,.— Sup.: excellentissima virtus,; : cultus,: triumphus,: aurum, et saep.—Adv.: excellen-ter, excellently, ; .—Comp., .—Sup.: excellentissime,.—
ex-celsus, a, um, P. a., elevated, lofty, high (freq. and class.; cf.: celsus, editus, altus, sublimis, procerus, arduus).
Lit.: mons,; cf.: vertex montis, * : locus,: porticus,: basis (statuae),; cf. signum,: statura,: aves (Ibes),: altitudo vineae, et saep.—Comp.: in excelsiore loco,: cornu (bovis),; cf.: crura chamaeleonis,.—Sup.: mons,; cf. locus,: rupes,: aegilops,; .—
Subst.
excelsum, i, n., a height: simulacrum Jovis in excelso collocare,; : Phoebus ab excelso, quantum patet, aspicit aequor,; so, ab excelso,: prohibebit in excelsum emicare (vitem),.—
Ex-celsus, i, m., the Highest, the Most High, i. e. God (eccl. Lat.), —
Trop.
In gen., high, lofty, distinguished, excellent, noble: te natura excelsum quendam videlicet et altum et humana despicientem genuit,; cf.: magnus homo et excelsus,: animus excelsus magnificusque,; cf. : excelso et illustri loco sita est laus tua,; cf.: te in excelsissimo humani generis fastigio positum, praef. § 11: species magnae excelsaeque gloriac, et saep.—Comp.: (orator) grandior et quodammodo excelsior,; cf. ; : quo tua in me humanitas fuerit excelsior quam in te mea,fin.—Sup.: excelsissimae victoriae,: duces,fin.—Subst.
, m.plur.: excelsi, ōrum, the lofty; prov.: excelsis multo facilius casus nocet, (Rib.).—
Neut.: excelsum, i, an elevated station or position: in excelso aetatem agere,i. e. in a high station,.—Esp. (eccl. Lat.): in excelsis, in the highest, in ascriptions of praise, —
Esp., in the later period of the empire, a title of high official dignitaries, e. g. of the praefectus praetorio, etc.—Adv.: excelsē, highly, on high, loftily.
Lit.: si vitis scandit excelsius,.—
Trop., in an elevated manner, highly: ornat excelse,: excelsius magnificentiusque et dicet et sentiet,: excelsissime floruit (Sparta),exceedingly,.

la:verb:excedo.gloss: to go out, go forth or away; depart, retire, withdraw; disappear
senses: to go out, go forth or away; depart, retire, withdraw; disappear
to overstep, overtop, overpass, rise above, go beyond; advance, proceed; transgress, digress
to depart from life; decease, die
to go beyond, surpass, exceed; tower above, overtop
la:verb:excedo.html:
ex-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3 (
subj. perf. sync. excessis, ), v. n. and a.
Neut., to go out, go forth or away, to depart, retire, withdraw (freq. and class.; cf.: discedo, deficio, destituo, desero, linquo, relinquo).
Lit.
In gen., with ex and abl., with abl. alone, or absol.: ex istoc loco,: e medio,: ex civitate,: ex Italia,: e templo,; for which, templo,: ex finibus,; for which, finibus,fin.; 7, 77, 14; ; : ex illa circumscriptione,

: ex itinere,; cf.: ex via,; for which, viā,: ex pugna, ex proelio,; ; for which, more freq., pugnā,; ; ; ; and, proelio,; ; fin.; 7, 80, 3; cf. acio,; ; : loco,; ; ; so, locis,; ; and bello,: domo,: oppido,; cf. urbe,; ; et saep.: Arimino,; : Galliā,: provinciis,: patriā,: sceleratā terrā, et saep.—With de (very rare): de utero matris,i. e. to be born,.—Absol.: abiit, excessit, evasit, erupit,: excedere deos, simul ingens motus excedentium,: primi omnium Macedones metu excesserant,—Designating the terminus: cave quoquam ex istoc excessis loco,: agro hostium in Boeotiam,: ex his tenebris in lucem illam,; cf.: ad deos,: invictum fore donec excederet ad deos,: in exsilium,; in which sense also simply excedere,.—

In partic.
To go beyond, overstep, rise above, overtop a certain boundary.—Of personal subjects very rarely: alter in Pontum, alter usque Aegyptum excessit,.—More freq. of inanimate subjects: ut nulla (pars) excederet extra,; ; cf. with eminere,: montes et excedentia in nubes juga,.—
To depart from life, to decease, to die (cf. decedo): sic ille cum undequadraginta annos regnavisset, excessit e vita,; so, e vita,; ; ; : vitā,; ; ; ; ; ; ; : e medio, Ruhnk.; and simply excedere (postAug.; but v. decedo excessus, I.),; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Trop.
In gen. (very rarely): cum animus Eudemi e corpore excesserit,; ; ; : corpore excedere,: ex pristina bellandi consuetudine, Auct. B. Afr. 73: palmā, to recede from victory, to yield the victory (= decedere alicui de victoria), .—Far more freq.,
In partic.
(Acc. to A. 2. a.) To go beyond a certain boundary or a certain measure, to advance, proceed, to transgress, digress (= procedere, progredi): mihi aetas ex magisterio tuo: : is postquam excessit ex ephebis, (quoted in ); cf.: ut primum ex pueris excessit Archias,: ad patres etiam et ad publicam querimoniam excessit res,; cf. : haec eo anno in Africa gesta. Insequentia excedunt in eum annum, quo, etc.,; cf. : paululum ad enarrandum, etc.,to digress,; cf.: in fabellam,: in aliquid,: res parva dictu, sed quae studiis in magnum certamen excesserit,; cf. ; ; cf. : eo laudis excedere, quo, etc.,to attain that height of fame,: tantum illa clades novitate et magnitudine excessit, i. e. exceeded, went beyond = eminuit, .—
(Acc. to A. 2. b.) To depart, disappear: cura ex corde excessit,: cum cupiditatum dominatus excessit,: jam e memoria excessit, quo tempore? etc.,; for which, memoriā,: ubi reverentia excessit animis,.— Poet.: Cannaene tibi graviorque palude Maeonius Stygia lacus excessere Padusque?i. e. have they slipped from your memory?.
Act. (post-Aug.).
Lit., to depart from, to leave a place: urbem,; ; ; 23, 1: curiam,; cf. pass. impers.: Crotonem excessum est,; fin.—
Transf., to go beyond, surpass, exceed a certain limit, to overtop, tower above (cf. above, I. A. 2. a., and B. 2. a.): nubes excedit Olympus,: statura, quae justam excederet,: summam octoginta milium,; so of numbers, very freq.,; ; ; ; ; cf. also of age,: triennium vitae,: annum aetatis centesimum,; ; ; ; of measure: laborum periculorumque modum,; so, modum,; ; ; : eloquentia aut aequavit praestantissimorum gloriam aut excessit,; cf.: praeturae gradum,: principum fastigium,: fastigium equestre,: excedente humanam fidem temeritate,; so, fidem,; : excessisse Priscum inmanitate et saevitia crimina, quibus, etc.,: nemine tantum ceteros excedente, ut ei aliquis se summitteret,.—With simple acc.: decretum, ne vasa auro solida ministrandis cibis fierent, etc. ... Excessit Fronto ac postulavit modum argento,went beyond the proposal, (cf.: egredi relationem,).—Pass.: duo enim multitudo, unione jam excessā,.
la:verb:excedo.inflection: cessi, cessum, 3, v. n. and a.

la:verb:excrucio.gloss: to torment greatly, torture, rack, plague; afflict, distress, harass, vex
senses: to torment greatly, torture, rack, plague; afflict, distress, harass, vex
to force out by torturing, extort
la:verb:excrucio.html:
ex-crŭcĭo, āvi, ātum, 1 (archaic
inf. praes. excruciarier, ), v. a., to torment greatly, to torture, rack, plague (class.).
Physically: perii! excruciabit me herus,: servos fame vinculisque,; cf.: (uxores) igni atque omnibus tormentis excruciatae,: aliquem vinculis ac verberibus atque omni supplicio excruciatum necare,; cf. also: hominem ingenuum fumo excruciatum semivivum reliquit,: excruciatus inopiā, Plaut Bacch. 3, 4, 24: ipsos crudeliter excruciatos interficit,: frigus nudos excruciabat, et saep.—Comic. Ep. Hunc tibi dedo diem. St. Meam culpam habeto, nisi probe excruciavero, qs. thoroughly torture it, i. e. use it up, make the most of it, .—
Transf., to force out by torturing, to extort: re excruciatā, —
Mentally, to afflict, distress, harass, vex, torment: conficior maerore, mea Terentia; nec meae me miseriae magis excruciant quam tuae,; cf.: non loquor plura, ne te quoque excruciem,: haec sunt, quae me excruciant,.—In imprecations: di deaeque te excrucient,: temeritas et libido et ignavia semper animum excruciant et semper sollicitant,: se,: quid illam miseram animi excrucias?; cf.: se animi,: tum Antipho me excruciat animi,; v. also in the foll.—In the pass.: excrucior,; : id ego excrucior,; cf.: hoc sese excruciat animi, Quia, etc.,.

la:verb:excubo.html:
ex-cŭbo, bŭi, bĭtum, 1, v. n.,
to lie or sleep out of doors.
In gen. (rare but class.): moniti Lacedaemonii, ut urbem et tecta linquerent armatique in agro excubarent,: apes noctu deprehensae in expeditione excubant supinae,.—
Trop.: Graeciam alienis sedibus,, v. Fittbogen ad h. l.—Far more freq.,
In partic., to lie out on guard, to keep watch, to watch.
Lit.: duae semper legiones pro castris excubabant,: legiones in armis,: legiones ad mare,: cohortes ad munitionem,: legio per muros,: excubitum in porta cohortes mittere,: Cerberus excubat ante fores,: quae (naves) ad portum excubabant,kept watch, et saep.—Poet.: (Cupido Chiae) Pulchris excubat in genis,sits on the watch, lurks,.—Of things as subjects: alni contra erumpentium amnium impetus riparum muro in tutela ruris excubant,: laurus ante limina excubat,.—
Trop., to watch, be watchful or vigilant, to be on the alert: cum Caesar ad opus consuetudine excubaret, etc.,: in navibus,: excubabo vigilaboque pro vobis,: sapiens semper animo sic excubat, ut nihil ei improvisum accidere possit,: curam rei publicae summae defendundae jam pridem apud vos excubare, is watchful, active, Planc. ap. : omnis eorum ars urbibus excubabat,i. e. was concerned, labored for the cities,.—Pass. impers.: rerum, non animi pretiis excubatur,care is exercised,.

la:verb:excutio.gloss: to shake out, shake off, elicit, knock out, drive out, cast off, strike off
senses: to shake out, shake off, elicit, knock out, drive out, cast off, strike off
to throw from or off of a horse, chariot, ship, etc.
la:verb:excutio.html:
ex-cŭtĭo, cussi, cussum, 3 (archaic
perf. subj. excussit, for excusserit, ), v. a.
quatio
, to shake out or off, to cast out, drive out, to send forth (class., esp. in the trop. sense).
Lit.
In gen.: posse ex his (litteris) in terram excussis annales Ennii, ut deinceps legi possint, effici,shaken out,: equus excussit equitem,threw off,: excussus equo,: excussus curru,; ; ; cf.: lectis excussit utrumque,: gubernatorem in mare e puppi,; cf. also: ancora ictu ipso excussa e nave sua,: lapide clavum,to knock off,: pulvis digitis excutiendus erit,: poculum e manibus,: ignem de crinibus,to shake off,: rem de manu alicujus,to strike out,: Pelion subjectā Ossā (Juppiter),: poma venti,to cast down, shake down, et saep.: ne nucifrangibula (i. e. dentes) excussit ex malis meis,to knock out,; cf.: cerebrum alicui,; : oculum alicui cyatho, verberibus,; ; cf.: oculo excusso,: ipso cum domino calce omnes excutiamus, to drive out or forth, Lucil. ap. : Teucros vallo,: hostem oppidis et regionibus,: ab obsidione Nolae urbis (with pellere a Campania),: feras cubilibus,to scare, rouse up,: si flava excutitur Chloë,be shaken off, cast off,: (viros) excussos patriā infesta sequi,: ut me excutiam atque egrediar domo,take myself off, decamp,: quartanas,to drive away, et saep.: (leo) gaudet comantes Excutiens cervice toros,shaking about, shaking,; cf. : caesariem,: pennas,: habenas,; cf.: nares inflare et movere ... et pulso subito spiritu excutere, etc.,to blow up, dilate,: se (gallinae edito ovo),: tela,to hurl, discharge,; cf. : fulmen in Thebas,: excussaque brachia jacto,tossed,; : (aër) Excussit calidum flammis velocibus ignem,sends out, produces,; cf. : largum imbrem (procellae), : lacrimas alicui,; : vomitum alicui,: sudorem, et saep.—Transf.: excutior somno,I am roused from sleep,; ; .—
In partic., to shake out, shake.
Esp. a garment, to free it from dust: vexatam solo vestem,; ; cf.: excutere de pulvere,shake yourself,; and: pulverem de pedibus,.—
To stir, move any thing to see under it; and hence, to search, examine a person: St. Di me perdant, si ego tui quicquam abstuli. Eu. Agedum, excutedum pallium, ; so, culcitisque et stragulis praetentatis et excussis,.—With personal objects: excutiuntur tabellarii, Asin. Poll. ap. ; cf.: verum (porcellum) ut subesse pallio contenderent Et excuti juberent,: non excutio te, si quid forte ferri habuisti: non scrutor,.
Trop.
In gen., to shake out or off, force away, etc.: omnes istorum delicias, omnes ineptias,to shake off, discard,: noli aculeos orationis meae, qui reconditi sunt, excussos arbitrari,plucked out, removed,: omnia ista nobis studia de manibus excutiuntur,are torn, wrested from our hands,; cf.: hanc excutere opinionem mihimet volui radicitus,: severitatem veterem,; cf. also: excutient tibi istam verborum jactationem,: excute corde metum,remove, banish,: diros amores,: orbem paci excutere,to banish peace from the world,: omnis quae erat conceptae mentis intentio mora et interdum iracundia excutitur,: quem (Senecam) non equidem omnino conabar excutere,: aliena negotia curo, excussus propriis,: dummodo risum excutiat sibi,can raise, produce,. —
In partic. (acc. to I. B.), to search, examine, inspect, investigate: explicando excutiendoque verbo,; cf.: pervulgata atque in manibus jactata et excussa, qs. shaken out, i. e. examined, . 26: illud excutiendum est, ut sciatur quid sit carere,: quae fere omnia Cicero in crimine veneficii excutit,; : totum locum,: aut conjecturā excutiuntur, an vera sint, etc., et saep.— Hence, excussus, a, um, P. a., stretched out, extended, stiff (post-Aug. and rare): interest, utrum tela excusso lacerto torqueantur, an remissa manu effluant,; so, lacerto,: palma excussissima,.—Adv.: excussē, strongly, violently: mittere pilam (with rigide, opp. languidius),.

Trop.
To improve, ennoble, refine, perfect (the class. signif. of the word): nihil tam horridum, tam incultum, quod non splendescat oratione et tamquam excolatur, prooem. § 3: C. Tuditanus omni vita atque victu excultus atque expolitus,; cf.: mansuefactus et excultus,: ex agresti immanique vita exculti ad humanitatem et mitigati sumus,: excultus doctrinā,; cf. ; : animos doctrina,: ingenia disciplinā exculta,: aetas exculta,: quibus rebus exculta hominum vita tantum distat a victu et cultu bestiarum,: inventas aut qui vitam excoluere per artes,: an victus hominum Atheniensium beneficio excoli potuit, oratio non potuit?; so, mores aut studia,: mores studiis,; ; : orationem,; : excultae cujusdam elegantiae,.—
Of persons, to honor (poet., and very rare, for the class. colere): deos,: aliquem,.

la:verb:excio.html:
ex-cĭo, īvi or ii, itum (long and short equally freq.; cf. excĭtus, Enn. ap. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; :
excītus,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; also acc. to cieo, ēre: excies, (R): exciet,; inf. exciere, ; imperf. excibat, : excibant,), 4, v. a., to call out or forth, to bring out: exciet, excutiet, Paul. ex Müll. To rouse, excite; to frighten, terrify any one: sopore,; cf.: excita anus, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 36 ed. Vahl.); cf. also: clamor subito ortus dictatorem quoque ex somno excivit,: somno excitus,: Mauri atque Gaetuli, ignoto et horribili sonitu repente exciti,: inter cetera, quae ad exciendum in Graeciam Antiochum dicere est solitus,: excivit ea caedes Bructeros, etc.,: qualis commotis excita sacris Thyias,; esp. freq. in the part. perf.; see the passages quoted init.; cf. also: (juventus) privatis atque publicis largitionibus excita, : ita conscientia mentem excitam vastabat,: Evander concursu pastorum, excitus,: Britanni omnium civitatium vires exciverant,.—Poet.: pulsuque pedum tremit excita tellus,frightened, quaking,; .—
